permission_purpose_map.scope: Precise, continuous, also when the app is closed
permission_purpose_map.rationale: Location fits delivery, but a customer usually needs it only while placing or tracking an order. Background, always-on collection is justified only as 'a better experience'.
Grocery delivery does not need your contact list. The stated use (social network analysis and recommending the app) serves the company, yet it is mandatory.
No voice feature is described. The only reason given is to 'improve our services', yet access is mandatory. If an optional voice-search feature existed, microphone access could fit it.
alternatives: Grant microphone only when using a voice feature, if one exists

consent_dimensions.explanation: Several purposes are vague ('improve our services', 'other business purposes', 'a better experience').
All permissions are presented as required; no optional uses are separated from delivery.
The text offers no separate choices for contacts, microphone or marketing sharing.
The notice treats continued use as agreement. Whether the app asks for a clear action cannot be seen without the consent screen.
No withdrawal route is described in the notice.
Recipients are unnamed categories and retention is open-ended.
Unrelated access is bundled with the core delivery service: the app will not work without it.

findings.title: Contacts and microphone made mandatory for grocery delivery
findings.explanation: The notice makes contacts and microphone access a condition of using the app, but neither is needed to deliver groceries. Contacts are used for social-network analysis and referrals; the microphone has no described feature.

evidence.text: SYNTHETIC DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT: QuickBasket is a fictional grocery delivery app invented for ConsentGuard demos. This is not a real policy.
When you create an account we collect your name, mobile number, email address and delivery addresses.

To use QuickBasket you must allow access to your precise location at all times, including when the app is closed, your phone contacts, and your microphone. If you do not allow these permissions the app will not work.
We collect location data continuously in the background to provide a better experience.
We use your information to deliver orders, process payments, improve our services and for other business purposes.
Contacts are used to help us understand your social network and recommend QuickBasket to people you know.
Microphone access helps us improve our services.
We may share your information with our partners, affiliates and other third parties for marketing and analytics.
We keep your information for as long as we consider necessary.
By continuing to use the app you agree to this notice.
For questions, write to the QuickBasket support team through the app.

legal_sources.title: Notification G.S.R. 843(E) appointing commencement dates for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
legal_sources.issuing_authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India
legal_sources.summary: On publication: s.1(2), s.2, ss.18-26, s.35, ss.38-43, s.44(1) and (3). One year after publication: s.6(9) and s.27(1)(d). Eighteen months after publication: ss.3-5, s.6(1)-(8) and (10), ss.7-17, s.27 (except (1)(d)), ss.28-34, 36, 37 and s.44(2).
legal_sources.applicability_notes: Controls which DPDP Act duties are in force on a given date.

legal_sources.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, rule 3 - Notice given by Data Fiduciary
legal_sources.issuing_authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India
legal_sources.summary: The notice must be understandable independently of other information; give in clear and plain language an itemised description of personal data and the specified purpose(s); and give a link and other means to withdraw consent with ease comparable to giving it, exercise rights, and complain to the Board.
legal_sources.applicability_notes: Commences eighteen months after publication of the Rules.

legal_sources.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, rule 8 - Time period for specified purpose deemed no longer served
legal_sources.issuing_authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India
legal_sources.summary: Specified classes of Data Fiduciaries must erase data after periods set in the Third Schedule (with 48-hour prior intimation); all Data Fiduciaries must retain processing logs and associated data for at least one year for purposes in the Seventh Schedule.
legal_sources.applicability_notes: Commences eighteen months after publication of the Rules. Note the one-year minimum log retention: a notice that mentions retaining some records for a year is not necessarily over-retention.

legal_sources.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 5 - Notice
legal_sources.issuing_authority: Parliament of India; text hosted by MeitY
legal_sources.summary: A consent request must be accompanied or preceded by a notice describing the personal data and purpose, how to exercise withdrawal and grievance rights, and how to complain to the Board; option to access the notice in English or an Eighth Schedule language.
legal_sources.applicability_notes: Commences eighteen months after G.S.R. 843(E). Applies to consent requests, not to processing on other grounds.

legal_sources.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 6 - Consent
legal_sources.issuing_authority: Parliament of India; text hosted by MeitY
legal_sources.summary: Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, limited to data necessary for the specified purpose (6(1)); illustration: contact-list access is not necessary for a telemedicine service. Withdrawal must be comparable in ease to giving consent (6(4)).
legal_sources.applicability_notes: Commences eighteen months after G.S.R. 843(E). Relevant only where consent is the basis of processing.

legal_sources.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 8(7) - Erasure
legal_sources.issuing_authority: Parliament of India; text hosted by MeitY
legal_sources.summary: Unless retention is necessary to comply with law, personal data must be erased on withdrawal of consent or once it is reasonable to assume the specified purpose is no longer served, whichever is earlier.
